title: LumenAI - Reserved Capacity Ops Eval
next_steps: Redwood to share reserved capacity pricing and commit tiers (Sophie) by 2025-10-10
Customer to provide peak qps and 95th/99th latency targets (Maria) by 2025-10-09
SE to run short prefix-cache benchmark on a 8xA10-like profile and share numbers (Diego) by 2025-10-14
Schedule technical deep-dive on VPC private control plane with Elaine and infra team (Sophie) for week of 2025-10-20
action_items: Sophie Chen: send reserved capacity contract template + example SLA matrix — due 2025-10-10
Diego Martinez: prepare mini benchmark (batching + KV cache) and include quantization options — due 2025-10-14
Maria Gomez: export current prod request distribution and 90/95/99 latency histograms — due 2025-10-09
Tom Baker: confirm networking constraints (eg no outbound internet, proxy limitations) and provide list of allowed IP ranges — due 2025-10-13
summary: Discovery call for reserved GPU capacity and isolation needs. LumenAI is evaluating Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private. Primary concerns: compliance (SOC2/ISO), VPC private control plane, predictable throughput for peak inference, burst strategy, and cost tradeoffs. Redwood AE/SE discussed autoscaling, burst pools, prefix/KV caching, quantization options, and routing fallbacks. Customer asked for benchmarks and pricing; next steps agreed on pricing, technical deep-dive and benchmark run.
transcript:
[00:00] Sophie Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — this is Sophie from Redwood, im the AE on this. quick roll call?
[00:07] Raj Patel: Raj here, CTO, LumenAI. morning.
[00:09] Maria Gomez: Maria, ML eng.
[00:11] Tom Baker: Tom, platform.
[00:13] Elaine Wu: Elaine, security/compliance.
[00:15] Diego Martinez: Diego, Redwood SE. good to meet you all.
[00:18] Sophie Chen: Cool — goal for today is to understand your production inference profile, isolation requirements, and what you mean by burst — then we'll map to Redwood hosted/dedicated/private options. should be ~45 minutes plus q&a.
[00:30] Raj Patel: Sounds good. Long story short we run LumenAI, we provide real-time summarization for enterprise docs. Latency SLO is low — 95p under 250ms for short prompts, but we also have longer multi-turn chat flows. Current infra is a mix of managed endpoints and some self-hosted GPUs. We're investigating a reserved pool because cost is spiking and we hit cold-start tails during big batch jobs.
[01:05] Maria Gomez: to add, our peak qps is pretty spiky — normal day 50 qps, but certain customers spike to 900 qps sustained for 10-20 minutes. We care about both p95 and p99. Also we do some embedding/semantic search jobs that are heavy but can be batched.
[01:30] Tom Baker: Network constraints: some of our largest customers require data never leave their VPC or require private connectivity. We're open to dedicated capacity with private networking.
[01:40] Elaine Wu: Security: SOC2 in progress, ISO on roadmap, need audit logs, KMS integration, SSO/SCIM. Also need a runbook for egress controls.
[01:50] Diego Martinez: Thanks. A couple quick Qs: what's your tolerance for some capabilities being slightly older — eg quantized model variants — versus always using the latest FP16 model? And what's your target for cost reduction?
[02:05] Maria Gomez: For customer-facing real-time, quality is non-negotiable; we can't degrade hallucination rates. For bulk offline tasks, we can accept quantized variants. We're looking to cut inference cost ~30-40% overall.
[02:20] Sophie Chen: Great — that maps nicely to a hybrid approach. Dedicated reserved pools for the real-time flows plus hosted fallback for overflow is a common pattern. We usually recommend a primary dedicated pool sized for 95p steady state and a burst pool for the delta. Redwood supports autoscaling with a reserved baseline and a configurable burst capacity that can tap into spare capacity or hosted variants.
[02:45] Raj Patel: Two things — first, how does the burst pool interact with private deployments? We can't have traffic route to fully public endpoints for some customers.
[02:55] Diego Martinez: If you go with Redwood Private (VPC/private control plane), burst can be configured within the same private deployment if you have spare physical capacity, or we offer controlled egress to a hosted fallback in regions you approve. There's also model fallbacks — if a larger model is too costly, requests can fallback to a smaller compatible variant with a retriable policy.
[03:20] Tom Baker: That fallback worries me — if we degrade model we may fail SLAs. Is there dynamic routing based on latency, cost, and customer tier?
[03:30] Sophie Chen: Yes, routing policies can be policy-driven. Example: gold customers only route to dedicated; silver customers can route to dedicated then to hosted fallbacks during bursts. You can also set hard caps to avoid fallback for certain routes.
[03:45] Maria Gomez: On the quantization front, can Redwood run int8 or 4-bit for our embeddings? Embedding quality must remain high.
[03:55] Diego Martinez: We have per-model quantization profiles and recommendations. For dense embeddings we usually avoid aggressive 4-bit unless validated. For decoder-only generation, 4-bit often works with negligible quality loss, but context-dependent. Part of the onboarding is a model QA pass and reference evals.
[04:15] Raj Patel: Ok. Walk us through how you'd size reserved GPUs for our workload. What inputs do you need?
[04:25] Diego Martinez: Key inputs: QPS distribution by prompt length, percent of requests that are streaming vs non-streaming, target p95/p99 latencies, average token lengths, and desired concurrency. Also what model variants you'll serve. With that we estimate GPU count and recommended instance types.
[04:40] Maria Gomez: We can share histograms. We currently run a mix: a 2B-generation model for short prompts and a 13B for longer flows. For embeddings we use a 3B encoder.
[04:55] Sophie Chen: Good. For the 13B flows you might want a higher-memory GPU or multi-GPU partitioning. Redwood supports assignment by model flavor. Also we can recommend splitting embedding and generation pools to optimize utilization.
[05:20] Raj Patel: What about pre-warmed KV/prefix cache? We do a lot of repeated prefixes.
[05:26] Diego Martinez: Automatic KV caching and prefix caching is available and can massively reduce token compute for repeated contexts. We can pre-warm hot keys and keep them in memory. For dedicated pools you control cache eviction policies.
[05:40] Tom Baker: Do you provide observability per-model per-route? I want token-level cost attribution.
[05:47] Sophie Chen: Yes, Redwood Console has per-route, per-model breakdowns, token-level cost and latency. You can export to your telemetry or we can push via webhook.
[05:55] Maria Gomez: On the VPC side — if we do Private deployment, who manages OS patching and kernel updates? We have strict change windows.
[06:05] Diego Martinez: For Private, customer can choose between a managed private control plane where Redwood handles OS/stack updates within agreed windows, or we provide an on-prem package where your ops team manages patching. We document maintenance windows and can stagger updates across nodes to avoid full pool churn.
[06:25] Elaine Wu: Encryption — we need KMS integration and customer-managed keys for both at-rest and in-transit. Also need audit logs for model invocations.
[06:35] Sophie Chen: We integrate with most KMS providers and can support HSM in dedicated/private offers. Audit logs for all inference requests are retained and can be forwarded to your SIEM; retention is configurable in enterprise plans.
[06:50] Raj Patel: Pricing — do you have example committed tiers? What's the delta vs pay-as-you-go hosted?
[06:58] Sophie Chen: Typical reserved pricing is X% cheaper than hosted payg depending on commit length and GPU type. For example a 12-month commit on a dedicated pool could be 30-50% lower unit cost vs on-demand hosted, but you trade commit and capacity reservation. We will send a matrix after this call tailored to the GPU types we recommend.
[07:20] Maria Gomez: Can you do short-term burst credits? Like guarantee reserve for baseline and then buy ad-hoc burst for spikes?
[07:28] Diego Martinez: Yes — we have burst credits and a burst pool concept; you can pre-purchase burst capacity or allow autoscaling to burst into marketplace/higher-cost pools. There's also a policy to cap burst spend per minute/hour.
[07:40] Raj Patel: If we needed absolute isolation for one large customer (no noisy neighbors) — is that possible with Dedicated?
[07:47] Sophie Chen: Fully yes. Dedicated can be single-tenant physical pools or isolated tenancy within a region. You can also reserve specific GPU classes. If you want air-gapped on-prem, Private on-prem is the option.
[07:58] Tom Baker: For our use-case, latency consistency is critical. What mitigation do you offer for tail latencies?
[08:05] Diego Martinez: Continuous batching with latency SLOs, prioritized scheduling, and per-request deadline enforcement. Also KV caching and hot-shard preloading helps tail behavior. For extreme tails, we can provision spare headroom and run warm replicas.
[08:20] Maria Gomez: How do you handle model upgrades and rollouts? Canary? A/B?
[08:26] Sophie Chen: We support canary deploys, traffic splitting, and automatic rollback based on configured quality metrics. You can pin routes to model versions and roll out gradually.
[08:36] Elaine Wu: Auditability for rollouts — need immutable logs of model version used per request for compliance.
[08:42] Diego Martinez: That's built-in — model version is attached to each request log. We can forward logs to your SIEM and preserve immutability for a configured retention.
[08:55] Raj Patel: What about failure modes — if a node fails mid-inference, how do you ensure consistency?
[09:02] Diego Martinez: The runtime supports checkpointed KV cache and request retries. For streaming requests, we have partial retry semantics and client SDKs can resume a stream from last ack. For critical flows we recommend multi-zone placement.
[09:18] Tom Baker: Multi-zone could add networking cost, though. Also curious about inter-AZ replication for cache.
[09:25] Diego Martinez: We do cross-AZ replication for KV metadata, but the full hot cache may be per-zone for performance. We can provide replication settings per pool.
[09:35] Maria Gomez: On benchmarking: we want to see p95/p99 on the 13B model for our prompt mix, and embedding throughput for the 3B.
[09:44] Diego Martinez: We'll need your sample prompts and a representative dataset. We can run a small-scale benchmark on a 4-8 GPU cluster with a matching instance profile and share numbers including throughput, cost per 1k tokens, and cold vs warm latencies.
[10:00] Raj Patel: Is there any long lead time to get Dedicated capacity live?
[10:06] Sophie Chen: Typical onboarding for dedicated reserved pools is 2-6 weeks depending on infra and networking approvals. Private on-prem can take longer (6-12 weeks) due to procurement and on-prem ops.
[10:18] Tom Baker: That timeline is ok. Our timeline: pilot in Q4, production roll in Q1.
[10:24] Maria Gomez: Ok — one more deep concern: cost predictability during unpredictable spikes. We don't want a surprise bill for a large one-off.
[10:33] Sophie Chen: You can configure hard caps and alerting. Reserved capacity covers baseline; for bursts you can set per-minute spend caps or require manual approval for very large bursts. Also committed monthly minimums smooth unit pricing.
[10:45] Raj Patel: Who at Redwood would be our primary technical contact during onboarding?
[10:50] Sophie Chen: Diego and Anya will be SE contacts; I'll coordinate contract and pricing.
[10:55] Maria Gomez: Great. About data retention — some customers require no request logs be stored. Can you support ephemeral logging?
[11:03] Diego Martinez: Yes, we support configurable retention and can disable persistent logs for routes. For compliance we'll note that some observability features may be limited if logs are disabled.
[11:12] Elaine Wu: We need an architecture review with our security team and SIEM owners.
[11:16] Sophie Chen: We'll schedule that — plan is a detailed security deep-dive with Elaine, and a VPC networking session with Tom.
[11:22] Raj Patel: Ok moving towards recap — what are the immediate asks?
[11:25] Sophie Chen: Recap: 1) LumenAI to share request histograms and prompt samples (Maria). 2) Redwood to share reserved pricing and example commit tiers (Sophie). 3) Redwood SE to run targeted benchmark on 13B and 3B profiles (Diego). 4) Schedule security and VPC sessions (Sophie + Tom + Elaine).
[11:42] Tom Baker: That works. One quick Q — do you have an SLA for p99 latency?
[11:46] Diego Martinez: We publish latency SLOs per GPU family for dedicated pools; SLAs are part of enterprise packages and can be tailored in Dedicated contracts.
[11:55] Maria Gomez: And support during incidents? We need 24/7 on-call for production issues.
[11:59] Sophie Chen: Enterprise support tiers include 24/7 on-call and a playbook with escalation paths. We'll include support tier options in the follow-up.
[12:08] Raj Patel: Nice. Anything else we should know?
[12:11] Sophie Chen: We'll also include a brief doc on cost optimization levers — recommended batching, per-route caching configs, and model variant suggestions.
[12:20] Maria Gomez: Perfect. Thanks everyone.
[12:22] Sophie Chen: Thanks all — we'll send the pricing and benchmark plan and follow up to schedule the security + VPC deep dives.
[12:30] Raj Patel: Thanks. Bye.
[12:33] (call ends)

Notes/Artifacts referenced: "sample prompt set" (customer to upload to shared drive), "reserved pricing matrix" (Redwood to provide), "mini-benchmark spec" (SE to provide).
Observed transcription oddities: 'KV cache' sometimes transcribed as 'K V cash', 'quantization' occasionally misheard as 'quanta station', speaker labels shifted briefly at 00:55-01:05.
